name: CPU logical core count
plain: Number of logical processors the browser may use.
meaning: Splits users into low, mid and high end hardware (2, 4, 8, 12, 16 or more threads). Sites use it to size worker pools; trackers use it as a stable hardware trait.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

fields.name: hardwareConcurrency
fields.precision: exact on Chrome and Edge; clamped or bucketed elsewhere

story.what_it_is: Tells a page how many processor threads your device can use.

marketing.name: Navigator.hardwareConcurrency
marketing.pitch: Docs explain it as a hint for how many parallel workers a page can sensibly start.

story.for_you: You never see it. It quietly decides how many tasks a site runs side by side. A strong laptop gets more, a budget phone fewer, which can mean faster and smoother pages.
story.for_makers: Apps need to know how many background workers to start without freezing the machine. The count also splits people into low, mid and high end groups. It is a stable number, so trackers like it.

use_cases.example: A browser video editor starts as many export workers as you have processor threads.
A browser game with many AI characters picks how many to simulate based on your thread count.
A large spreadsheet app in the browser spreads calculations across workers.
A video call app decides how many video streams to decode at once.
A code editor in the browser sizes its background search pool to your hardware.
A fraud tool notes that a supposed phone reports 64 threads and flags a server.
An ad network treats a device with 16 threads as a higher spending hardware tier.

risks: Hints at how wealthy a device is

technical_bounds: Value is logical threads, not physical cores
Safari and Firefox protections vary by mode and script
